rationales.1: On desktop this is the fastest catalog of the four, with right-aligned prices, inline stock, season sections, and filter chips. On mobile two rows collapse into one-word-per-line columns, which destroys at-a-glance reading for those products.
rationales.2: Quantity steppers with an add button on every row plus a conventional product page keep the money path exactly as convention dictates, with prices where shoppers look for them.
rationales.3: This arm is the most honest of the set: the estimated rate is flagged, out-of-stock carries a restock promise, the price-pending line invites a note instead of showing a number, and the footer explains the test-tray provenance of every figure.
rationales.4: The one-word-per-line wrapping of the carrot and sweet pea entries at phone width is a real failure for older readers, and the minus and plus stepper targets are small; elsewhere type is legible and hover-free.
rationales.5: Type hierarchy and section rhythm are handsome, but the narrow-column wraps visible even on desktop for two rows, and the broken mobile columns, are exactly the arbitrary misalignments craft discipline forbids.
rationales.6: The product page is the strongest for deciding: year table, an at-a-glance strip for difficulty, germination, and height, unhurried growing notes, and companions with reasons and links.
rationales.7: The potting bench with seasonal drawers and a vouch-for-everything promise is a coherent signature true of a two-person shop, though it shapes the page less totally than the almanac arm.
rationales.8: Novelty lives in the bench metaphor and the voice while every commerce mechanic stays textbook-conventional, matching a brand-layer-only break budget.
rationales.9: If it is listed, we can vouch for it, and the easiest drawer on the bench are the best sentences on any arm; the visible design-study disclaimer in the footer is the one line a real shop would never print.
rationales.10: Filter chips, inline stock, and add controls on the list make a repeat purchase the fastest here, and the restock promise serves the shopper who came back for the carrot.
